questions.prompt: A user clicks the top cell in column 2. Where does the token go?

options.label: Into the lowest empty cell in column 2.
Into the clicked top cell.
Into the lowest empty cell in any column.

questions.explanation: Clicking identifies a column; the illustrated rule applies gravity within that column. The chosen row is determined by occupancy, not by pointer height.

questions.prompt: What happens when the selected column is full?

options.label: Reject the move and preserve the current player.
Overwrite its top token.
Switch to the next column automatically.

questions.explanation: A full column has no legal insertion point. Changing columns or overwriting silently changes the move, while changing the player would consume a rejected turn.

questions.prompt: How must directional counting treat the newly placed token?

options.label: Count it once, then scan outward in both directions.
Count it once for each side and add both totals unchanged.
Ignore it because it was not on the previous board.

questions.explanation: Starting at one and adding matching neighbors avoids double-counting the center. Counting it in both directions can incorrectly declare a three-token run a win.

questions.prompt: Can the next player move after a winner is displayed?

options.label: No; terminal state rejects all further moves.
Yes; only the winner message is final.
Only if they choose a different column.

questions.explanation: Stopping is a core requirement. Guard the transition as well as disabling controls so programmatic calls and queued events cannot mutate a finished game.

questions.prompt: What is the meaning of a stack index in the column-stack approach?

options.label: Index 0 is the bottom token in that column.
Index 0 is always the top rendered row.
It identifies the player rather than the cell.

questions.explanation: The stack appends upward from the bottom. A rendered row r maps to stack index ROWS - 1 - r; using r directly inverts gravity.

questions.prompt: Does indexed winner detection make the full stack-based move constant time?

options.label: No; projecting stacks into a matrix still visits the board.
Yes; every array copy disappears.
Yes; React renders only the winning window.

questions.explanation: The small set of candidate windows limits detection, but matrix projection and rendering still touch board cells. State the cost of the complete operation separately.

questions.prompt: When is the board a draw?

options.label: Every cell is occupied and no winner was found.
Whenever a column is full.
Whenever both players have equal token counts.

questions.explanation: A successful-move count detects total occupancy. Winner detection takes precedence on the final move; a full column or balanced counts alone says nothing about a draw.

questions.prompt: Put this baseline implementation recipe in dependency order. Each step prepares the next.

items.label: Preserve terminal state or advance the turn

questions.explanation: First establish the input and state contract, then implement the dependent transformation, and finally validate the observable result. Reversing these steps risks testing a UI whose rules or input identity have not been defined. This order is a rehearsal recipe, not the only possible engineering workflow.
